messages.subject: std.lv = TRUE changes model interchangeability?
messages.body_plain:
I have a measurement model and a structural model, both with the same paths - only difference is covariance vs regression arrows:

mod_meas <- '
  ## latent variable definitions (CFA)
  HOME_t1 =~ b1 * accept_t1 + b2 * variety_t1 + b3 * acStim_t1
  HOME_t2 =~ b1 * accept_t2 + b2 * variety_t2 + b3 * acStim_t2

  ## covariances
  HOME_t1 ~~ HOME_t2 + adhd_t1 + adhd_t2
  HOME_t2 ~~ adhd_t1 + adhd_t2
  adhd_t1 ~~ adhd_t2

  ## autocorrelations
   accept_t1 ~~ accept_t2
  variety_t1 ~~ variety_t2
   acStim_t1 ~~ acStim_t2

  ## self-regression
  adhd_t1 ~ 1 * adhd_t1
  adhd_t2 ~ 1 * adhd_t2
'

fit_meas <- cfa(mod_meas, data = adhd_home_env,
                std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)

mod_struct <- '
  ## latent variable definitions (CFA)
  HOME_t1 =~ b1 * accept_t1 + b2 * variety_t1 + b3 * acStim_t1
  HOME_t2 =~ b1 * accept_t2 + b2 * variety_t2 + b3 * acStim_t2

  ## regression
  HOME_t2 ~ HOME_t1 + adhd_t1
  adhd_t2 ~ adhd_t1 + HOME_t1

  ## covariances
  HOME_t1 ~~ adhd_t1
  HOME_t2 ~~ adhd_t2

  ## autocorrelations
   accept_t1 ~~ accept_t2
  variety_t1 ~~ variety_t2
   acStim_t1 ~~ acStim_t2

  ## self-regression
  adhd_t1 ~ 1 * adhd_t1
  adhd_t2 ~ 1 * adhd_t2
'

fit_struct <- sem(mod_struct, data = adhd_home_env,
                  std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)

Then why is there a difference in Chi-squared? (But not in df...)
anova(fit_struct, fit_meas)
#> Chi-Squared Difference Test
#>
#>            Df    AIC    BIC  Chisq Chisq diff Df diff Pr(>Chisq)
#> fit_struct 16 6635.8 6710.8 31.559
#> fit_meas   16 6643.5 6718.5 39.304     7.7452       0
#> Warning message:
#> In lavTestLRT(object = new("lavaan", version = "0.6.7", call = lavaan::lavaan(model = mod_struct,  :
#>   lavaan WARNING: some models have the same degrees of freedom

When setting std.lv <http://std.lv> = FALSE gives the expected results - but also I loose a df, why?
Why does std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE break the interchangeability between the models?

fit_meas <- cfa(mod_meas, data = adhd_home_env,
                std.lv <http://std.lv> = FALSE)
fit_struct <- sem(mod_struct, data = adhd_home_env,
                  std.lv <http://std.lv> = FALSE)

anova(fit_struct, fit_meas)
#> Chi-Squared Difference Test
#>
#>            Df    AIC    BIC  Chisq Chisq diff Df diff Pr(>Chisq)
#> fit_struct 15 6634.2 6712.9 27.995
#> fit_meas   15 6634.2 6712.9 27.995 -7.636e-10       0
#> Warning messages:
#> 1: In lavTestLRT(object = new("lavaan", version = "0.6.7", call = lavaan::lavaan(model = mod_struct,  :
#>   lavaan WARNING: some restricted models fit better than less
#>   restricted models; either these models are not nested, or
#>   the less restricted model failed to reach a global optimum.
#> 2: In lavTestLRT(object = new("lavaan", version = "0.6.7", call = lavaan::lavaan(model = mod_struct,  :
#>   lavaan WARNING: some models have the same degrees of freedom

messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaan group,

I am a little bit desperate about the following problem: I am trying to find out, what impact does the agreement between leaders and subordinates regarding the leadership behaviours of a manager have on the perceived quality of team processes.

I three measured variables: y=Perceived leadership behaviours (level 1: subordinates ratings, IV), x=self-rated leadership behaviours (level 2: leaders self-ratings,IV) and z=perceived quality of team processes (level 1: subordinates ratings,DV).

I already understood that I need to do a polynomial regression with Response Surface Analysis to test the different effects of agreement. Thus, I created squared versions of my two independent variables (x2, y2) and one interaction (xy) and also defined the parameters. Variables are centered by grand mean. Since the data are clustered, I wanted to run a ML model. Later on I would like to extend the model, as to test another hypothesis my DV needs a latent change model (I want to examine the amount of change).

I started with a null model, and then I ran a random intercept model. Both worked.
nullmodell<-'

level:1

z~~z

level:2

z~~z'

rimodel<-'

level:1

z~xy.c+y.c+y2.c+x.c+x2.c

level:2

z~~z'

To examine if I need random slopes I wanted to compare a random slopes and random intercepts model. However, if I try to fit the random slopes model, I get following error:

rsmodel<-'

level:1

z~xy.c+y.c+y2.c+x.c+x2.c

level:2

z~x.c+x2.c'
rsmodel.fit<-sem(rsmodel, data=b1, cluster="Code", fixed.x = FALSE, estimator="MLR")

lavaan ERROR: initial model-implied matrix (Sigma) is not positive definite;  check your model and/or starting parameters.

My data have no missing values and lavaan is updated (0.6-7). My data do only contain 337 observations; the cluster size is very sparse, ranging from 1-12 employees per manager. Is that the source of the error?

Best regards,

David

messages.body_plain:
Thank you so much Patrick!
You helped and guided me to the right path!
I've got two questions after reading:
1. In all the examples I have found, the age groups are divided into people of exactly the same age. In my study, I have subjects aged 65 and over (92). It seems to me worthwhile to divide them into 5-year-old groups, otherwise it will be too much. But then, to what number do I set their constrains? (when it's possible with equal age groups to set the second group to start from 2 if you have two- years gap between them, for example. In my case, there is no exact gap between every two people in different groups)
2. Do you know an example in R? I have so far found only in mplus, where one can simply insert the word cohort. Do you have any idea how to write it in lavaan? (Assumes manual writing is needed)

Hi there,

Thanks again for your previous help. I generated the population data for the four groups and ran sim with that data. This seemed to work.
I then tried to use this information to find power using varying sample sizes through getPower. My goal here is the find power for each parameter estimate for the actual sample sizes we have for each of the four groups. And to determine the sample sizes necessary for each parameter estimate at 80% power.

However, I'm running into another issue. When I  use the getPower function, I'm provided with an object containing only one variable. Then when I pass that through findPower, I get the following error: Error in powerTable[, ivCol] : incorrect number of dimensions. I thought perhaps this was because the object I obtained through getPower was not a dataframe. So, I changed it to a dataframe and then received the following error when trying to use findPower:  Error in findPower(pow, "N", 0.8) :
  Cannot find the specified target column. I have tried naming "N" as the variable name I get from the getPower dataframe (which is "V1") but I get the same error message. I appreciate any guidance you can provide. Thank you so much!

Here is my syntax for the population models, simulation, and power estimates

##Simulate population models for each group and combine into dataframe
popDatamodela <- simulateData(popModela, sample.nobs = 10000)
popDatamodelb <- simulateData(popModelb, sample.nobs = 10000)
popDatamodelc <- simulateData(popModelc, sample.nobs = 10000)
popDatamodeld <- simulateData(popModeld, sample.nobs = 10000)

popData <- rbind(popDatamodela, popDatamodelb, popDatamodelc, popDatamodeld)
popData <- data.frame(popData, group = rep(c(1, 2, 3, 4), each = 100000))

##estimate sample model from population data
Output.a <- sim(5, modelH2, n=list(200,200,200,200), rawData = popData, group = "group", std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, lavaanfun = "sem") ##using nRep=5 in order to identify error, actual number will be much higher

##Obtain power
pow <- getPower(Output.a, alpha = 0.05, nVal=c(200,200,200,200), pmMCAR = c(0, 0.1, 0.2)) ###The 'pow' object/dataframe contains only one variable
findPower(pow, "N", 0.80)
>>Error in powerTable[, ivCol] : incorrect number of dimensions

pow <- data.frame(pow)
findPower(pow, "N", 0.80)
>>Error in findPower(pow, "N", 0.8) : Cannot find the specified target column

messages.subject: How can I get “cfi.robust” instead of “cfi.scaled” in ordered CFA ?
messages.subject_clean: How can I get “cfi.robust” instead of “cfi.scaled” in ordered CFA ?
messages.body_plain:
As Terrence mentioned on another log, “The correct calculation of robust fit measures proposed by Brosseau-Liard & Savalei (2014) has only been proposed for mean-adjusted chi-squared statistics (estimators MLM, MLR, WLSM, ULSM), not mean- and variance-adjusted (or "scaled & shifted") statistics (estimators MLMV, WLSMV).  WLSMV is the default for ordinal data, so that is why cfi.robust, rmsea.robust, etc., will be NA.  The *.scaled fit measures are simply using the original formulas for non-robust chi-squared, but plugging in the robust chi-squared (which, as the articles explain, will not be consistent estimators of the true population values).”

 So, I think that “cfi.robust” is the better fit index than “cfi.scaled” because cfi.robust will be consistent with the true population value. Is my understanding right?

 Then, I wrote the following R code and conduct it. But I can get the error message.

 ******************************************************************************************

configural.fit <- cfa(model, data=combined.dat, estimator="MLM", group="ng",

                      ordered=c("O1", "O2","N.O3", "O4", "O5", "N.O6",

                                "N.SP1", "N.SP2", "N.SP3", "N.SP4", "N.SP5","N.SP6",

                                "N.CP1", "CP2", "N.CP4",

                                "CP3", "CP5", "CP6",

                                "N.SS1", "N.SS2", "N.SS3", "N.SS4", "N.SS5","N.SS6",

                                "CS1", "CS2", "CS3"))

 Error in lav_options_set(opt) :

  lavaan ERROR: estimator ML for ordered data is not supported yet. Use WLSMV instead.

 **************************************

I set the estimator as “MLM”, but lavaan did not recognize it.

Would you tell me what is wrong on my R code?

Then, would you tell me how to get “cfi.robust”?

Sincerely,

Hideki

messages.subject: Exogenous control/covariate variables CFA
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I would like to model a latent variable (let’s call it L) that captures the shared variance of three measured indicators (M1-M3). For one measured indicator M1, I would like to control for the effect of three size measures (S1-S3) so that I get the effect of M1 (corrected for S1-S3) on L. Schematic figure is attached.

In a linear regression approach, I would do: M1~S1+S2+S3 and extract the residuals. So I could enter in the sem model resid(M1), but is it possible to control for the effect of S1-S3 on M1 directly in the SEM model? If I simply add a regression in the SEM model like this:

L =~ M1 + M2 + M3

M1 ~ S1 + S2 + S3

it shows me the path coefficients of S1-S3 on M1 and from L on M1, but the path coefficient of L on M1 is not corrected for size. Is it possible to model it in SEM and if yes how?

Thank you in advance for your help!

Best,

Magali

messages.body_plain:
Magali,

is this what you meant to type? "get the effect of M1 (corrected for S1-S3) on L" -- because you're modeling M1 as an indicator of L--i.e., effect of L on M1.

In any case, the M1 part of your diagram shows a multiple regression of M1 on S1, S2, S3, and L. This includes L as a simultaneous cause of M with the Ss. If L were observed, this should show results comparable to your linear regression idea. But since L is latent and defined in part by M1, there's no obvious analog.

Pat

messages.subject: Re: How can I get “cfi.robust” instead of “cfi.scaled” in ordered CFA ?
messages.subject_clean: How can I get “cfi.robust” instead of “cfi.scaled” in ordered CFA ?
messages.body_plain:
Hideki,

The "robustness" in MLM/MLR is robust with respect to deviations from normality in the outcomes. Using WLSMV estimator means such deviations are not applicable to ordered outcomes--with the probit link they are modeled as reflections of an underlying continuous normal variable. As the error told you, "estimator ML for ordered data is not supported yet." So WLSMV is the best bet even if it's not perfect.

If this is critical to you, I believe Mplus can estimate ML with ordinal data by numeric integration.

Pat

messages.subject: Baseline model specification
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm wondering if I've run into a possible bug in how the baseline model is specified in lavaan. Or I don't understand the rationale for one option vs. the other. I include reproducible code below, however the fundamental issue is this:

Model 1: use "fixed.x = FALSE" command in sem() and only regression terms in model object gives:

Model Test User Model:

  Test statistic                                11.107
  Degrees of freedom                             5
  P-value (Chi-square)                     0.049

Model Test Baseline Model:

  Test statistic                               165.608
  Degrees of freedom                               9
  P-value                                              0.000

model1@baseline$partable$ustart includes the exogenous covariance

Model 2: identical to Model 1 except explicitly include exogenous variance/covariance terms in model object gives:

Model Test User Model:

  Test statistic                                11.107
  Degrees of freedom                                 5
  P-value (Chi-square)                           0.049

Model Test Baseline Model:

  Test statistic                               165.944
  Degrees of freedom                                10
  P-value                                        0.000

model2@baseline$partable$ustart does not include the exogenous covariance

So, why is the exogenous covariance part of the baseline model in Model 1 but not in Model 2?

Thanks,
Leslie

Reproducible code follows:
# principles and practice of sem (4th ed.), rex kline
# recursive path model of illness, figure 7.5 (p. 159), table 4.2
library(lavaan)

# input the correlations in lower diagonal form
rothLower.cor <- '
   1.00
    -.03 1.00
     .39  .07 1.00
    -.05 -.23 -.13 1.00
    -.08 -.16 -.29  .34 1.00 '
# name the variables and convert to full correlation matrix
rothFull.cor <- getCov(rothLower.cor, names = c("exercise","hardy","fitness",
                                                "stress","illness"))
# display the correlations
rothFull.cor
# add the standard deviations and convert to covariances
rothFull.cov <- cor2cov(rothFull.cor, sds = c(66.50,38.00,18.40,33.50,62.48))

# path model 1 - fixed.x = FALSE
roth.model1 <- '
  # regressions
  illness ~ fitness + stress
  fitness ~ exercise
  stress ~ hardy'

reduced1 <- sem(roth.model1,
               sample.cov=rothFull.cov,
               sample.nobs=373, fixed.x = FALSE, sample.cov.rescale = FALSE)
summary(reduced1, fit.measures = TRUE, rsquare = TRUE)
parameterestimates(reduced1)
fitmeasures(reduced1, fit.measures = c("chisq", "df"))

reduced1@baseline$test$standard$stat

# path model 2 - fixed.x = FALSE & variance terms specified
roth.model2 <- '
  # regressions
  illness ~ fitness + stress
  fitness ~ exercise
  stress ~ hardy
  exercise ~~ exercise
  hardy ~~ hardy
  exercise ~~ hardy'

reduced2 <- sem(roth.model2,
               sample.cov=rothFull.cov,
               sample.nobs=373, fixed.x = FALSE, sample.cov.rescale = FALSE)
summary(reduced2, fit.measures = TRUE, rsquare = TRUE)
parameterestimates(reduced2)
fitmeasures(reduced2, fit.measures = c("chisq", "df"))

reduced2@baseline$test$standard$stat

messages.subject: EBM Factor Scores
messages.body_plain:
Hello lavaan group,

I currently have a CFA with four latent variables that are indicated by a mix of continuous and binary manifest variables. I have estimated the CFA using WLSMV, which fits well (CFI=0.955, RMSEA=0.035, SRMR=0.069), and would like to obtain an estimate of factor scores for each of the four latent variables.

>From looking through prior threads and papers I have decided to use the Empirical Bayes Modal method since some of my manifest variables are binary.

I have two questions, which I cannot seem to find answers to in the lavaan documentation or literature. First, is the EBM method as applied in lavaan appropriate for models with mixtures of continuous and binary variables? Second, there are a few cases that are missing on all manifest variables for a single latent variable (but not completely missing as they have observed data on manifests for other latent variables). However, these cases still have factor scores estimated for the latent variable for which they have no observed manifest variables. Are these factor scores usable? This seems in contrast to the "ML" method, which returns factor scores of 0 if all manifests are missing for a latent variable.

My code is below:

cog4f <- '
# latent variables
mem =~ v1 + v2 + v3 + v4 + v5 + v6 + v7 + v8
lan =~ v9 + v10 + v11 + v12 + v13 + v14 + v15 + v16 + v17
vis =~ v18 + v19 + v20
exfx =~ v21 + v22 + v23 + v24 + v25

# covariance of latent variables
mem~~lan + vis + exfx
lan~~vis + exfx
vis~~exfx

# residual covariances
v1~~v5
v6~~v1
v5~~v6
v20~~v19
v2~~v7
v3~~v8
'
cog4f.fit <- cfa(cog4f, data=mi, estimator="WLSMV", missing="pairwise", ordered=c("v10", "v11", "v12", "v13", "v14", "v15", "v16", "v17", "v18"), parameterization="delta")

ebm <- lavPredict(cog4f.fit, type="lv", method="EBM")

Thank you in advance for your help.

Joseph

messages.subject_clean: How can I get “cfi.robust” instead of “cfi.scaled” in ordered CFA ?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Pat,

Thank you very much for your comment. I understand that ULS and WLS estimators should be used for ordinal data.

Although WLSMV is set as a default estimator, there are other variants such as WLSM, ULSM, WLSMVS, ULSMV, ULSMVS as described in the following table.  I would like to know which is the best among them. If WLSMV is the best, I would like to know the reason why it is considered the best among the several variant estimators.

Then, there are two adjusted fit measures for ordinal data such as *.scaled and *.robust. Which one should be referred as fit measures for ordinal CFA?  Only WLSM and ULSM give us both *.scaled and *.robust measures as described in the table.  If *.robust measures is better than *.scaled ones, should we use WLSM or ULSM instead of WLSMV?

 Would you please give me any suggestions about them?

Sincerely,

Hideki
2021年3月3日水曜日 1:39:11 UTC+9 mal...@malonequantitative.com:

> Hideki,
>
> The "robustness" in MLM/MLR is robust with respect to deviations from normality in the outcomes. Using WLSMV estimator means such deviations are not applicable to ordered outcomes--with the probit link they are modeled as reflections of an underlying continuous normal variable. As the error told you, "estimator ML for ordered data is not supported yet." So WLSMV is the best bet even if it's not perfect.
>
> If this is critical to you, I believe Mplus can estimate ML with ordinal data by numeric integration.
>
> Pat
>
> On Tue, Mar 2, 2021 at 2:06 AM 岡林秀樹 <hideki.okab...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Thank you very much for your suggestion.
> >
> > I understand that we should use WLSM, ULSM, and WLSMV estimator for ordered variables.
> >
> > I confirmed which estimator gets which goodness of fit (“*.robust and *.scaled” or “scaled” only).
> >
> >
> >      WLSMV is a default estimator for ordered variables. But it can get only scaled fit measures.
> >
> >      If the scaled fit measures will not be consistent estimators of the true population values as Terrence suggested
> >
> >     and robust fit measures are better than scaled fit measures, we should use WLSM or ULSM to get robust fit measures instead of using WLSMV.
> >
> >      How do you think about this?
> >
> >      My question is which fit measures is the best for ordered CFA (scaled or robust).
> >
> >      Then, which estimator is the best for ordered CFA?
> >
> >
> >
> > Sincerely,
> >
> > Hideki
> >
> > 2021年3月2日火曜日 12:00:25 UTC+9 rpc...@psu.edu:
> > > You’ve declared your variables as ordered but you are using an estimator that requires (or assumes) they are continuous. If you want to use MLM, then remove the ordered argument. Of course, that may not be a good idea if the variables really do need to be treated as ordered.
> > >
> > > Sent from my iPhone
> > >
> > > > On Mar 1, 2021, at 9:49 PM, 岡林秀樹 <hideki.okab...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > ﻿
> > > >
> > > > As Terrence mentioned on another log, “The correct calculation of robust fit measures proposed by Brosseau-Liard & Savalei (2014) has only been proposed for mean-adjusted chi-squared statistics (estimators MLM, MLR, WLSM, ULSM), not mean- and variance-adjusted (or "scaled & shifted") statistics (estimators MLMV, WLSMV).  WLSMV is the default for ordinal data, so that is why cfi.robust, rmsea.robust, etc., will be NA.  The *.scaled fit measures are simply using the original formulas for non-robust chi-squared, but plugging in the robust chi-squared (which, as the articles explain, will not be consistent estimators of the true population values).”
> > > >
> > > >  So, I think that “cfi.robust” is the better fit index than “cfi.scaled” because cfi.robust will be consistent with the true population value. Is my understanding right?
> > > >
> > > >  Then, I wrote the following R code and conduct it. But I can get the error message.
> > > >
> > > >  ******************************************************************************************
> > > >
> > > > configural.fit <- cfa(model, data=combined.dat, estimator="MLM", group="ng",
> > > >
> > > >                       ordered=c("O1", "O2","N.O3", "O4", "O5", "N.O6",
> > > >
> > > >                                 "N.SP1", "N.SP2", "N.SP3", "N.SP4", "N.SP5","N.SP6",
> > > >
> > > >                                 "N.CP1", "CP2", "N.CP4",
> > > >
> > > >                                 "CP3", "CP5", "CP6",
> > > >
> > > >                                 "N.SS1", "N.SS2", "N.SS3", "N.SS4", "N.SS5","N.SS6",
> > > >
> > > >                                 "CS1", "CS2", "CS3"))
> > > >
> > > >  Error in lav_options_set(opt) :
> > > >
> > > >   lavaan ERROR: estimator ML for ordered data is not supported yet. Use WLSMV instead.
> > > >
> > > >  **************************************
> > > >
> > > > I set the estimator as “MLM”, but lavaan did not recognize it.
> > > >
> > > > Would you tell me what is wrong on my R code?
> > > >
> > > > Then, would you tell me how to get “cfi.robust”?
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Sincerely,
> > > >
> > > > Hideki

messages.body_plain:
Hi Pat,

Thank you
for you quick reply. Indeed I meant the effect of L on M1.

So if I
understand correctly it is not possible to model L as a simultaneous cause of M1 with the S1-S3 (so combining a latent construct with a linear regression). So the only way to model this would be to extract in a first
step the residuals from a linear regression (M1~S1+S2+S3). And in the second
step using the residuals of M1 next to M2 and M3 in the latent construct.

A short
follow-up question: In a composite construct (as in the attached figure), it
would be similarly impossible to model the simultaneous effect of V (with the
Ss) on C in lavaan? So here again a workaround would be to extract in a first

messages.body_plain:
A couple of thoughts about your approach here.

I would make sure the simulation includes all sample sizes you're planning to compute power for. It looks like one of your group sizes is 44, but the smallest sample size in a group you're looking at is 50. Ideally the smallest sample size used in the simulation would be below the smallest N of interest.

In all your simulations you're assuming equal group sizes for each replication (N in all groups is either 50, 51, etc.)*

You're only using 51 replications. For stable estimates of power you need many more replications, ideally 1000+ or even 5000+. You could change the n option to be: list(rep(50:100,100),rep(50:100,100),rep(50:100,100),rep(50:100,100)) this will give you 5100 replications.

* The way getPower is currently built it will only use the overall N from the model to compute power in a situation where N varies across replications. This isn't ideal for a multiple group model (and it's something we need to fix) since you can arrive at the same total N with different N per group and that might have an impact on power. I think for now your approach is a good one, but be aware that your power analysis has an assumption that doesn't match your data.

Alex

> A couple of thoughts about your approach here.
>
> I would make sure the simulation includes all sample sizes you're planning to compute power for. It looks like one of your group sizes is 44, but the smallest sample size in a group you're looking at is 50. Ideally the smallest sample size used in the simulation would be below the smallest N of interest.
>
> In all your simulations you're assuming equal group sizes for each replication (N in all groups is either 50, 51, etc.)*
>
> You're only using 51 replications. For stable estimates of power you need many more replications, ideally 1000+ or even 5000+. You could change the n option to be: list(rep(50:100,100),rep(50:100,100),rep(50:100,100),rep(50:100,100)) this will give you 5100 replications.
>
> * The way getPower is currently built it will only use the overall N from the model to compute power in a situation where N varies across replications. This isn't ideal for a multiple group model (and it's something we need to fix) since you can arrive at the same total N with different N per group and that might have an impact on power. I think for now your approach is a good one, but be aware that your power analysis has an assumption that doesn't match your data.
>
> Alex

messages.body_plain:

I have a couple of questions regarding the use of runMI.

1.  I am running a very simple factor analysis model and when I run it with cfa.mi, everything works just fine.  However, when I run it with lavaan.mi, I receive the message.

Error in lav_model_estimate(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavpartable = lavpartable,  :
  lavaan ERROR: initial model-implied matrix (Sigma) is not positive definite;
  check your model and/or starting parameters.

Error in if (attr(x, "se") == "robust.huber.white" && attr(x, "information.meat") != : missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed

I presume this means that MLR doesn't work with runMI, but then does this mean that I can't handle non-normality and missing data using multiple imputation?  Do I have to resort to FIML and MLR?

Thanks

David

messages.subject: About composite variables-based models
messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

My ultimate research aim is to identify whether one or multiple aspects (i.e. indicators)  of  "CURRENT BODY STATE"  mediate the interaction between  one or multiple  indicators of "PREVIOUS BODY STATE"  and one or multiple  indicators of "PERFORMANCE" .
Hypothesis: Only some indicators from  "CURRENT BODY STATE" but not all of them  play a key role in the  interaction between "some" indicators (but not all) from PREVIOUS BODY STATE"  and "some" indicators (but not all) from "PERFORMANCE".

Two aspects are important to keep in mind: First, despite the fact that indicators represent clustered data (i.e. correlation between the indicators of each variable), it is critical to determine (i.e., quantify) their individual roles. Second, the  nature of the indicators captures the full universe of the variables. Namely, the variables are entirely made up of the indicators. For this reason, I think I need to model my data with composite variables instead of latent ones.

Question1:  Would you agree with my rationale? Or, is it rather more appropriate/efficient to model a latent variable-based model?

Assuming that composite variables modelling is the right way to go,  two preliminary steps would implement two different multilevel models to  identify those indicators with significant values in the regressions.

Step A. Multilevel regression inspecting the interaction between the indicators of "CURRENT BODY STATE"   and the indicators of "PERFORMANCE".

Step B. Multilevel regression inspecting the interaction between the indicators of "PREVIOUS BODY STATE"   and the indicators of "PERFORMANCE".

To note, I did not check the interaction: "PREVIOUS BODY STATE" - "CURRENT BODY STATE" because my study is focused on "PERFORMANCE". Thus, any indicator with no significant interaction with another indicator from "PERFORMANCE", would be beyond the scope of this study.

Question 2:   Is this way the most efficient one?  Or would you rather suggest  any other option to identify the "main" indicators (i.e., those with significant associations)?

Subsequently in step C,  I would compute a composite variables-based model  including only those indicators with significant values.

Question 3:  Again, if composite variables are the right direction, I wonder how I could get a "clear" example of computing such composite variables with lavaan. It is my understanding that this package does not do this automatically.

Many thanks in advance,

Julian Gaviria
Neurology and Imaging of cognition lab (Labnic)
University of Geneva. Campus Biotech.
9 Chemin des Mines, 1202 Geneva, CH
Tel: +41 22 379 0380
Email: Julian.Ga...@unige.ch

messages.subject: Re: Covariances results
messages.body_plain:
Not scaling of the covariances, but of the variances of the latents. The variance of a latent is undefined without an additional constraint. There are multiple ways to impose the constraint. cfa() by default (you didn't show us your function call) does so by fixing the loading of the first indicator of each latent to 1. I don't have direct knowledge of what AMOS does, but the other common standard in CFAs is to constrain the latent's variance to 1.

You can look to the variances sections of your output to see this.

The resulting models are equivalent.

messages.subject: Re: Covariances results
messages.body_plain:
What you have going on in that you have to set a scale to identify a latent variable. Usually that means that you either set the first indicators factor loading to 1 or set the variance of the latent variable to 1. If you set the variance of the latent variable to 1, then that latent variables is standardized. If you did that in Amos, but in Lavaan did it differently, the covariances would be different, but the correlations would be the same. The reason why is that the correlations come from the standardized solution which is setting the variances of the latent variables to 1. So make sure that in both Amos and Lavaan that in the covariances or unstandardized solution that the first factor loading is set to 1 (default in both) and the factor variances are freely estimated. That should fix it.

What you are describing is not a Toeplitz matrix, you need to have the same diagonal variance across for it https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toeplitz_matrix

Further this becomes a simple thing to paramterize. You can see that mplusautomation gives the code for it in mplus that can easily be trnstaed to lavaan

> library(MplusAutomation)
> mplusRcov(letters[1:4], "toeplitz", "rho", "e", FALSE)
a b c d (e);
a WITH b (rho);
b WITH c (rho);
c WITH d (rho);
a WITH c (rho2);
b WITH d (rho2);
a WITH d (rho3);

in lavaan

a ~~ e*a
b ~~ e*b
c ~~ e*c
d ~~ e*d

a ~~ rho*b
b ~~ rho*c
c ~~ rho*d
a ~~ rho2*c
b ~~ rho2*d
a ~~ rho3*d

Dear All,

Do please forgive my simplistic question. But in my reproducible example below, is it possible NOT to estimate the intercepts for the dummy variables Group_HI and Group_MT?

(In fact, is it necessary to estimate them?)

Many thanks,

library(tidyverse); library(fastDummies)

d <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rnorouzian/v/main/memory.csv")
d <- dummy_cols(d, "Group")[-7]

model <- "MP ~ Group_HI
   SE ~  Group_HI
   MP ~  Group_MT
   SE ~  Group_MT
   Group_HI ~~ 0*Group_MT
   MP ~~ MP
   SE ~~ SE
   MP ~~ SE"

sem(model, data = d, meanstructure = TRUE)

Intercepts:

   .SE                4.200    0.256   16.413    0.000
    Group_HI          0.385    0.067    5.701    0.000
    Group_MT          0.327    0.065    5.026    0.000

messages.body_plain:
The p-value is computed under the null. What you have is estimation under the alternative. Bootstrap is inherently an estimation method, not a testing method. (There's Bollen-Stine bootstrap... which is Beran-Srivastava bootstrap... under the null; but you have to make some strong assumptions that you can rotate your data as you please with it.) You can get bootstrap standard errors, but that's not the bootstrap p-value.

messages.subject: Why are my SEM-estimates of this simple model biased?
messages.subject_clean: Why are my SEM-estimates of this simple model biased?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I generated data (n=1 Mio) based on linear equations with predefined parameters and random noise. Then I applied a SEM on this data and expected to obtain estimates that are the same as my predefined paramters.
However some of these estimates are biased, especially
the one that is affected by my binary categorical engogenous variable dx (me~dx, de~dx)
the estimated threshold | of this binary categorical variable dx
I am also wondering why SEM finds a small correlation between 'me' and 'de', which should not be related according to my definition. Could this be a reason why the estimates are off?

Can someone please explain why I am getting these biased estimates from sem()? Is this expected or is there an error in my minimal example? Below is my code.

Thanks in advance for ay help!

Best,
Jana

library(semTools)
library(lavaan)

#set.seed(42)
n_new_samples = 1000000

model_sm='
  dx ~ a + ap + s
  me ~ dx + a
  de ~ dx + a + s
'

#Generate exogenous variables
#Z-transform numeric variables
s_a = scale(runif(n_new_samples, 45, 98), center = TRUE, scale = TRUE)
s_ap = rbinom(n_new_samples, size=1, prob=0.4)
s_s = rbinom(n_new_samples, size=1, prob=0.5)

c1 = 0.4
c2 = 0.2
c3 = 0.1
th=0.5
c4 = 0.2
c5 = 0.2
c6 = 0.1
c7 = 0.03
c8 = 0.5

#Generate Endogenous with pre-chosen coefficients
s_dx = ifelse((c1*s_a + c2*s_ap + c3*s_s + rnorm(n_new_samples, mean=0, sd = 1))>=th,1,0)
s_me = c4*s_dx + c5*s_a + rnorm(n_new_samples, mean=0, sd = 1)
s_de = c6*s_dx + c7*s_a + c8*s_s + rnorm(n_new_samples, mean=0, sd = 1)

#Assemble data frame with synthetic data
synth_df_fac = data.frame(a = s_a, s = factor(s_s), ap = factor(s_ap),
                          dx = factor(s_dx, ordered=TRUE), me = s_me, de = s_de)
#Fit SEM
fit= sem(model_sm, data=synth_df_fac, meanstructure=TRUE)
summary(fit)

#Compare SEM-estimates with predefined parameters
predef_params = c(c1, c2, c3, c4, c5, c6, c7, c8, th, NA,NA, NA, NA, NA)
result = data.frame(endo=parTable(fit)$lhs[1:14], op = parTable(fit)$op[1:14],
                    exo = parTable(fit)$rhs[1:14],
                    est=parTable(fit)$est[1:14],
                    predef = predef_params)
result

messages.subject: Binary outcomes: missing interaction values
messages.body_plain:
Hello there,

I am encountering a problem when I try to fit a model on binary outcome data for a moderated mediation model. I get the error message:  lavaan ERROR: some variables have no values (only missings) or no variance
The variable in question for which I do not get any values is the interaction term op_id:op_rep (see code example below). This issue does not appear when I have an interval scaled .
Do you have any recommendations how I can fix this issue? Any help is highly appreciated!

Best,
Niklas

Below, you find the code to replicate my issue:

library(tidyverse)
library(lavaan)

# Generate Data
set.seed(161)
N = 300
a1 = .3
b1 = .1
b2 = .05
b3 = .4
c1 = .3

int <- rep(c(0,1), N/2)
op_id <- rnorm(N)
op_rep <- a1 * int + rnorm(N)

## Binary DV
eq <- b1 * op_rep + b2 * op_id + b3 * op_rep * op_id + c1 * int
p_int_com <- 1/(1+exp(-eq))
int_com <- rbinom(N, 1, p_int_com)
int_com <- ordered(int_com, levels = 0:1)

## Interval Scaled DV
int_perc <- b1 * op_rep + b2 * op_id + b3 * op_rep * op_id + c1 * int + rnorm(N)

df <- tibble(int = int, op_id = op_id, op_rep = op_rep, int_perc = int_perc, int_com = int_com)

# Logarithmic Model
model_log_simp <- '
             # effects on criterium
             int_com ~ b1 * op_rep + b2 * op_id + b3 * op_rep:op_id + c1 * int
             # effects on mediator
             op_rep ~ a1 * int

             # indirect effects conditional on moderator
             indirect.low := a1 * (b1 + b3 * (0 - 1)) # 0 - 1 = mean - SD
             indirect.high := a1 * (b1 + b3 * (0 + 1))

             # direct effect
             direct := c1

             # total effects
             total.low := direct + indirect.low
             total.high := direct + indirect.high

             # proportion mediated
             prop.mediated.low := indirect.low/total.low
             prop.mediated.high := indirect.high/total.high
            '

fit_log_simp <- sem(model_log_simp,
           data = df,
           ordered = "int_com",
           se = "bootstrap",
           estimator = "DWLS",
           bootstrap = 5000
           )

# Linear Model
model_lin_simp <- '
             # effects on criterium
             int_perc ~ b1 * op_rep + b2 * op_id + b3 * op_rep:op_id + c1 * int
             # effects on mediator
             op_rep ~ a1 * int

             # indirect effects conditional on moderator
             indirect.low := a1 * (b1 + b3 * (0 - 1)) # 0 - 1 = mean - SD
             indirect.high := a1 * (b1 + b3 * (0 + 1))

             # direct effect
             direct := c1

             # total effects
             total.low := direct + indirect.low
             total.high := direct + indirect.high

             # proportion mediated
             prop.mediated.low := indirect.low/total.low
             prop.mediated.high := indirect.high/total.high
            '
fit_lin_simp <- sem(model_lin_simp,
           data = df,
           se = "bootstrap",
           bootstrap = 5000
           )

messages.body_plain:
Hi! I was wondering how to deal with mean differences among latent variables. For example, I have two models below. They are very different (multiple groups vs. single group, huge difference in the number of parameters to estimate). model1 doesn't have good fit, however, model2 has an acceptable fit.

> model1<-'
        LV1 =~ item_1+item_2+item_3+item_4
        LV2 =~ item_5+item_6+item_7
        LV3 =~ item_8+item_9+item_10
        LV1 ~~ LV2
        LV2 ~~ LV3
        LV1 ~~ LV3
'
> cfa(model1, data=data, group="myGroups",
         group.equal =c("loadings","intercepts","lv.variances", "residual.covariances","residuals"), meanstructure=T)

> model2<-'
        LV1 =~ item_1+item_2+item_3+item_4
        LV2 =~ item_5+item_6+item_7
        LV3 =~ item_8+item_9+item_10
        LV1 ~~ LV2
        LV2 ~~ LV3
        LV1 ~~ LV3
        LV1 ~ grp2 + grp3 + grp4
        LV2 ~ grp2 + grp3 + grp4
        LV3 ~ grp2 + grp3 + grp4
' # grp2-grp4 are dummies.
> sem(model2, data=data)

My questions are:
1. If I assume there are groups in the sample, is the multiple group approach a more appropriate way to start?
2. Since model2 fit is good, can I report model2 as a way to compare mean differences across the four groups (grp1-grp4, using grp1 as reference)? If I report it, can I interpret it as the way we interpret in multiple regression?

Thank you for your help!!!

Dear all,

as the Mplus discussion forum seems to be disabled at the moment (for whatever reason) and most of you are also quite familiar with Mplus too, I would like to post the following question here:

Still using modification indices (for WLSMV) in my CFA, I recognized that standardizing latent variables in the MODEL statement results in identical estimates under the MODEL RESULTS and STANDARDIZED MODEL RESULTS sections, which is in line with my expectations.
However, under MODEL MODIFICATION INDICES the StdYX E.P.C. differs from E.P.C. and/or Std E.P.C., but only for WITH Statements (ON/BY exhibit uniform EPCs).
Concerning correlated error terms (which I focus my analyses on) now I wonder which of these EPC values can or should be regarded as standardized?

I did not inspect this issue in other software like e.g. lavaan, but I would expect it to be identical as it seems to me rather a "fundamental" modeling/estimation/parameterization aspect than a software feature.

Thanks (again) in advance & kind regards,
Jan

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,
I am a masters student trying to run a SEM model in lavaan for the first time.
I have got this error message:
lavaan WARNING: some observed variances are (at least) a factor 1000 times larger than others; use varTable(fit) to investigate

I was wondering what does this mean for my data, after some reading I saw some recommendation about scaling certain columns?

Any input on the matter would be appreciated

Also, please do let me know if you need more information.

Emily

messages.subject: Re: Error warning in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
hi Emily,

I believe it is acceptable to scale down the variable that has this higher variance, by dividing that variable in your dataframe by some constant. The data itself doesn't change, just the unit (e.g. if you had measured age in days, dividing by 365 yields age in years (well, apart from the issue that 365 is an approximation, given leap years etc.) )

klaas

messages.subject: error with reliability() and HTMT()
messages.body_plain:
Hello !
I am working on the UTAUT2 model that discusses why people use technology. I used Lavaan and semTools for the model. I have a problem with reliability() function , always showing the error :

Error in ly[[i]] %*% ve[[i]] : non-conformable arguments
In addition: Warning message:
In (apply(ly[[i]], 2, sum)^2) * diag(ve[[i]]) :
  longer object length is not a multiple of shorter object length

and HTMT() always showing the error:
Error in as.character.default(x) :
  no method for coercing this S4 class to a vector

Is there a problem of the data set this way? It consists of results of the components for latent variables and the observable variables. My sample size is 162. and my model is as follows:

model_1 <- '
  # variables
    PE =~ pe1 + pe2 + pe3
    EE =~ ee1 + ee2 + ee3 + ee4
    SI =~ si1 + si2 + si3
    FC =~ fc1 + fc2 + fc3
    HM =~ hm1 + hm2 + hm3
    H =~ h1 + h2 + h3
    IU =~ iu1 + iu2 + iu3
    PV =~ pv1 + pv2 + pv3
    PVV=~ pvv1 +pvv2
    PPR=~ ppr1 +ppr2 +ppr3
    PPP=~ ppp1 +ppp2 +ppp3
    PIN=~ pin1 +pin2 +pin3

  # regressions
    PV ~  PPP + PVV + PPR
    IU ~ PE + EE + SI + FC + HM + PV + H
    use ~ IU
    pa ~ use

'
UTAUT2 <-data.frame(UTAUT)
UTAUT_2 <- scale(UTAUT2)
fit <- sem(model_1, data = UTAUT_2)

summary(fit, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

messages.subject: reliability of p-values of standardizedSolution
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm running several analysis with lavaan and encountered some strange p-value differences in my analysis. Using the summary(model...)-function, I do get a significant path with a p-value of .03. Looking at the standardizedSolution, however, the I get a p-value of ~.5 for the exact same path.
Based on some of the discussions in this forum I did get the impression that p-values for standardized parameters using the stand.Sol.-function can be trusted. Somewhere else, I read that one should report standardized coefficients paired with p-values of the unstandardized solution. Thus, I'm a bit confused now and would appreciate any suggestions by the experts of this forum.
Thanks in advance.
Jan

messages.subject: Re: reliability of p-values of standardizedSolution
messages.body_plain:
Jan,

Disclaimer: I haven't used stand.Sol.

Broadly speaking in SEM, the unstandardized solution should be used for hypothesis tests.

Consider that the unstandardized path coefficient is a single parameter estimate with its standard error.

The standardized path coefficient is that estimate, multiplied by another point estimate treated as an exact value, and divided by yet another point estimate treated as an exact value.

So the standardized estimate has much more room for deviation from the population value built into it.

That said, that large a discrepancy is unusual and might warrant further investigation (e.g., are the standard errors of the variance estimates very large).

Pat

messages.subject: Re: Unweighted Least Squares
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I know this was quite an old topic. I came across this topic, when I was trying to understand how to interpret an (unknown) and "NA"  chi-square p-value. I was also running an ordinal CFA model with the ULS estimator for 51 Likert-scale items responded on a 5-point scale, which with 11 subscales. The sample size a bit small, N=240. All the other indexes that I am checking seems fine to me,  χ² (1169) =1653.35, p = NA, CFI= 0.98, TLI= 0.98, RMSEA= 0.04, SRMR= 0.07, with significant factor loadings-standardized values ranging from 0.54 to 1.00.

Should I report it as I did above or just mention that "It is recommended to 'avoid' reporting (unscaled) chi-square test statistics in results of a CFA, if the "ULS" was used as an estimator." and not mention about it? Should I refer to this discussion group as a reference or anyone knows/has a paper on this?

Thanks,

Almer

On Friday, 28 June 2013 at 12:15:50 UTC+2 yros...@gmail.com wrote:
> On 06/25/2013 09:14 AM, John Taylor wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > While running various ordinal CFA models I noticed that the p-values
> > were specified as "(unknown)" and "NA" when ULS was used. I have
> > searched through the postings and noticed it was mentioned that ULS is
> > not distributed as a chi-square asymptotically and was wondering if that
> > was the reason for no p-value calculated or if there is some other reason.
>
> That is the reason indeed. We try to 'avoid' that users report
> (unscaled) chi-square test statistics in their papers if estimator="ULS".
>
> > Also, I have seen various references that robust estimation methods like
> > ULSMV are appropriate for continuous variables, but are they appropriate
> > for ordinal variables? I ask because mainly because I am surprised that
> > my models are showing worse fit if I specify the variables as ordinal
> > and use a robust method like ULSMV versus if I use ULS. This is
> > surprising because my sample size is large (n=1236) and my items are
> > univariate normal, though not multivariate normal.
>
> That is an interesting observation. I looked for papers/sources that
> could shed some light on this but could not find anything.
>
> Anyone else?
>
> Yves.

messages.subject: Re: reliability of p-values of standardizedSolution
messages.body_plain:
If someone is interested in why the p value differs between different scaling approaches, this paper explains it quite nicely.

Gonzalez, R., & Griffin, D. (2001). Testing parameters in structural equation modeling: Every “one” matters. Psychological Methods, 6(3), 258–269. https://doi.org/doi:10.1037/1082-989X.6.3.258

If you want to get a p value that is not affected by latent variable scaling, you can fit a model were the focal parameter is constrained to be zero and do a likelihood ratio test between the constrained model and the original model.

Mikko

messages.subject: Re: Why are my SEM-estimates of this simple model biased?
messages.subject_clean: Why are my SEM-estimates of this simple model biased?
messages.body_plain:
Jena,
This was an interesting question.  I was hoping someone would spot something simple.  Did you get an answer off list?
If not, here are the strategies that I would follow:

1. Pare down the model in various ways to find the minimal sufficient model to reproduce the difference between expected and obtained estimates. (For example, I tried fixing the threshold and still obtained similar results.)  Try removing some of the variables and or parameters to simplify the example.

2. There may be some misspecification if you are simulating data based on observed dichotomous variables but the model is estimating effects based on implicit latent continuous variables.  You might try simulating the data using the simulateData() function from the lavaan package.  This would help ensure consistent interpretation of the model between data simulation and parameter estimation.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

> no significant mediation has taken place across all levels of QhDSttmn right?

None of the individual comparisons with the reference category are significant.  If you want an omnibus test, use lavTestWald() to test the constraint that all 9 "a" paths == 0.

Maybe the lowest negative slope is significantly different from the highest positive slope.  But if this is just post hoc fishing, you should correct for multiple (9) tests.

>
> > Sobel test has suffered and probably succumbed to a lot of criticisms.
>
> FYI, lavaan does not provide the Sobel test.  The Sobel test assumes that a and b have uncorrelated sampling distributions.  lavaan uses the delta method, which takes that correlation into account.  So it will work better than the Sobel test regardless, and the delta method yields nominal Type I error rates in sufficiently large samples.  The Monte Carlo method Mauricio mentioned is much less computationally intensive and works about as well as bootstrapping in smaller samples (but both break in small samples, for different reasons).

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone.

I am conducting analysis to calculate latent mean differences between three groups. For doing so, I am comparing group 1 with group 2, group 2 with group 3 and then group 1 with group 3.
In doing so, I am using the lavPredict function (see the syntax below), everything work smooth; however, I am hesitating why the estimated means of groups differ even though I am using the same data, why does it happen?

Could someone help me to explain this please because I am not sure how to report the mean values if they are different.

thanks in advance.

LOC1: M = 49.79346 / LOC2: M = 52.91117

LOC2: M = 51.33574 /LOC3: M = 52.11754

LOC1: M = 51.10342/ LOC3: M = 50.36060

master$LOCATION <- factor (master$LOCATION,
                           levels = c(1,3),
                           labels = c("LOC1", "LOC3"))

MG.model <- eqMI.main(model = mediation.model.compare,
                      data = master,
                      group = "LOCATION",
                      meanstructure = TRUE,
                      output = "both", #mean, covariance, both
                      equivalence.test = FALSE, #change this in a moment
                      adjRMSEA = TRUE, #but see new paper
                      projection = TRUE, #see notes
                      bootstrap = FALSE)

predicted_scores <- lavPredict(MG.model$convention.sem$LavaanOut$fit.strict.residuals,
                               type = "ov")
table(master$LOCATION)
predicted_scores <- as.data.frame(do.call(rbind, predicted_scores))
predicted_scores$LOCATION <- c(rep("LOC1", 257), rep("LOC3", 370))
predicted_scores$sum <- apply(predicted_scores[ , 1:15], 1, sum)
tapply(predicted_scores$sum, predicted_scores$LOCATION, mean)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Guiseppe,

How did you form your product indicators? probe2WayRC is designed for residual centered (orthogonalized) product indicators. If you used another method it won't function correctly, that's probably the reason for the error. If you used mean centering for product indicators (or double mean centering) then the probe2WayMC function is a better choice. In either case you shouldn't need to include residual covariances between the original items and the product terms in your model.

Alex

messages.subject_clean: Multilevel Mediation in Lavaan, centering of variables
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I want to perform Multilevel Mediation Analyses in R with Lavaan, but I came across a Problem:

Normally, at least that is what I've learned, it is important to group-mean center level-1 variables and grand-mean center level-2 variables for multilevel analyses. So that's what I did when trying to do multilevel mediation in lavaan as well.

Not surprising, I got tons of errors when first trying, but after lots of troubleshooting, I simply went for the non-centered variables and it worked perfectly.

So my question is: Is it not necessary to do group/grand-mean centering for multilevel mediation analyses in lavaan (maybe because Lavaan does the centering itself by default)?

Thanks in advance for you help!

messages.body_plain:
> I did not know how to fit three groups simultaneously

There is no restriction in lavaan on the number of levels in a multigroup model (although typically there are only a few groups).

https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/groups.html

Here is a strict-invariance example with 4 groups:

HS <- HolzingerSwineford1939
HS$school.sex <- interaction(HS$school, HS$sex)
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '
fit.strict <- cfa(HS.model, data = HS, group = "school.sex",
                  group.equal = c("intercepts", "loadings","residuals"))

messages.subject: Re: Multilevel Mediation in Lavaan, centering of variables
messages.subject_clean: Multilevel Mediation in Lavaan, centering of variables
messages.body_plain:
> it is important to group-mean center level-1 variables and grand-mean center level-2 variables for multilevel analyses.

Only predictors.  If you group-mean-center the outcome, there can be no Level-2 variance.   And if you group-mean-center a predictor, then its Level-2 component (i.e., the cluster means) will not be able to explain any Level-2 variance unless you also include that as a predictor.  The advice in MLM to do mean centering is entirely dependent on how you want to interpret coefficients (and variance components), so you wouldn't mean-center dummy codes, because 0 already has a useful meaning.

> So my question is: Is it not necessary to do group/grand-mean centering for multilevel mediation analyses in lavaan (maybe because Lavaan does the centering itself by default)?

lavaan automatically separates the within and between components of Level-1 variables, so there is no need.  But since you can have fixed-effects of exogenous Level-1 variables that do not appear in the Level-2 model (see the ?Demo.twolevel help-page example), you could very well cluster-mean-center them if you wanted.  Regardless, yes you can grand-mean-center exogenous Level-2 variables if you want to be able to interpret the intercept that way.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
